turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Tom Brennan? In you come. I did the observations outside, blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-four, temperature thirty-six point six.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Is there a chair that isn't a torture device? I'm wrecked.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit on the edge of the couch if that's easier, Tom. I'm Dr Keane. Who's with you today?
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Siobhan Doyle. I do his home help three mornings a week, and I drove him. He couldn't face the bus.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand. What's the main trouble, then?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The lower back. It's been a few weeks and it's doing my head in. I can barely get the boots on for work.
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): A few weeks my eye. It's since the move, Tom.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The move was, look, the bad pain is a few weeks. Don't be adding on the whole spring.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Ye moved the first week of May. That's six or seven weeks of him groaning every morning.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): So I'm hearing anything from a few weeks up to about seven, and ye don't agree. I'll park the exact start. Where does it sit, and what's it like?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Across the bottom, worse on the left. A deep ache, and if I bend to lift a bucket it shoots down the back of the left leg.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): How bad, on a normal day?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Desperate in the mornings. Maybe a seven out of ten. By evening if I've been plastering I'm fit for nothing. Um, sitting is worse than walking, actually.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): I have to ask the awkward red-flag things one by one, so bear with me. Any numbness or a dead feeling in the legs, or around the saddle, between the legs?

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Saddle, no, nothing strange there. The left foot though, after the van it feels a bit dead, not numb numb. I walk it off and it's grand. I don't know if that even counts.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll note the foot as a maybe. Any trouble with the waterworks, leaking, or not knowing when the bladder is full?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Same as always. I go when I go.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever, sweats, feeling flu-y with this?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I'm just tired because I'm not sleeping with the ache. That's different.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): And weight. Have you lost weight without trying?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I have not. I'm eating less takeaway since the move, that's all. The trousers are the same.
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): They're not the same. You've dropped weight, the jeans are hanging off you since April. I see you every week.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah Siobhan, the jeans were always big. I have not lost weight. Leave it.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so the two of ye disagree on the weight as well. I won't treat that as a fact either way. What are you taking for the pain?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two tablets when it's bad. I think they're the five hundred milligram ones, and sometimes I just forget and suffer through it.
[SEG0026] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The chemist told him to take them regular, four times a day. He doesn't. He skips most of them.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Because they barely touch it. What's the point.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else, anti-inflammatories, anything stronger?

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I was on naproxen, five hundred milligrams twice a day, and I stopped it in March. It was burning the stomach. They wrote me a prescription for tramadol once, and I never took it, never even brought the script to the chemist.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the naproxen is stopped, and the tramadol was never taken. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0032] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Penicillin. His mother told me he came out in a rash as a child and he's to avoid it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): That was not an allergy. It was a heat rash, and I've had penicillin since, for a tooth, no bother. I'm not allergic.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll record that there's a dispute on penicillin and a rash, not a clear allergy. Let me have a look at the back. Can you stand?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Slowly. Yeah. Go on.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're tender over the left lumbar muscles. Flexion is limited, you stop about halfway. Straight leg raise is clear on both sides, no nerve stretch. Power and feeling in the feet are intact today.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): See, the foot's fine now. I told you.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): You did. Thinking out loud, this could be straightforward mechanical low back pain, it could be a bit of disc irritation with that shooting pain, and I am not going to call it anything sinister. No cauda equina picture on what you've said. I won't conclude past a working impression.
[SEG0039] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He had an X-ray of the back in A&E in April, after he slipped on the path. They said it was fine.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): That was before this, and it was a waste of an afternoon.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): I was going to send you for a lumbar X-ray today. Hearing that, there's no sense repeating it. Scratch the X-ray.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): So what, I just live with it?

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. My working impression is mechanical low back pain with referred pain into the left leg. A disc is still possible, I can't rule that out from the couch. We'll get you to physiotherapy rather than more pictures now.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Physio. Grand, if they can see me before Christmas.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to community physio. And we might do an MRI if this has not settled in six weeks. Not booking it today.
[SEG0046] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Should he be off the plastering?

[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Light duties if the boss will allow it, and don't take to the bed. Bed rest makes these worse. Keep walking, short walks, and a bit of heat on it in the evening is reasonable.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Heat I can do. The walking, when I'm not wrecked.

[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Try the paracetamol properly, two of the five hundreds four times a day with food, not just when you're desperate. If the stomach plays up we leave the naproxen off, I'm not restarting that.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I'm not taking the naproxen anyway.

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks, whether or not physio has started. If you suddenly can't pass urine, or the saddle goes numb, or the leg gives way, that's the same day, A&E, not waiting on me.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. I hear you.
[SEG0053] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll make sure he actually comes. And I'll write the paracetamol times on the fridge, for what it's worth.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't be writing on the fridge like I'm ninety.
[SEG0055] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the physio referral from out here, and a review slot in a fortnight. Mornings are quieter if the back is worse then.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning, yeah. Not too early. I'm a pain in the mornings, ask her.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): Morning is fine. Anything else you wanted to ask before you go?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I be able to go back plastering full time? I've a job on in Rathmines and they're already giving out.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can't promise a date. Most of these settle over weeks if you keep moving. If it's no better when I see you, then we look at that scan. Not before.
[SEG0060] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Come on, Tom. The car's on a meter.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks. I suppose.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

bad.reason: Driving detail wrong: transcript says after the van, not explicitly driving.
bad.text: Left foot feels dead after driving (category=neurological, status=present, severity=mild, frequency=after driving, temporality=current, body_site=left foot, aggravating_factors=driving, relieving_factors=walking, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

bad.reason: Completed A&E April X-ray supported, but requested_by caregiver is not stated.
bad.text: Lumbar spine X-ray (type=imaging, status=completed, requested_by=caregiver, indication=back pain after a slip, done in A&E in April)

omissions.text: Low back pain is worse in the mornings and improves relative to evening pattern only insofar as by evening after plastering he is 'fit for nothing'; walking is better than sitting.
Patient can barely get his boots on for work because of the back pain.
Negative finding asked and answered: no sweats or flu-like feeling with the back pain.
Negative finding asked and answered: patient denied unintentional weight loss; weight loss was disputed rather than simply present.
Paracetamol use was recorded inaccurately: patient said he takes two tablets when bad and thinks they are 500 mg tablets, not confirmed 500 mg.
Stopped naproxen in March because it was burning his stomach.
Tramadol had been prescribed once but was never taken and the prescription was never filled.
Lumbar flexion detail: he stops about halfway.
Doctor explicitly stated there was no cauda equina picture based on the history given.
Planned lumbar X-ray was cancelled after learning an April A&E back X-ray after a slip was normal; no repeat X-ray planned.
Follow-up timing nuance: return in two weeks whether or not physiotherapy has started.
Nurse planned to book the physiotherapy referral and review slot in a fortnight, with mornings preferred because the back is worse then.

bad.reason: Patient denies allergies, but transcript says penicillin allergy is disputed, not absent.

omissions.text: Patient denied leg numbness/dead feeling apart from a possible transient left foot dead feeling after being in the van; this specific red-flag question about leg numbness was asked and overall not recorded as a negative finding.

Paracetamol current use is incompletely/wrongly recorded: patient takes two tablets when pain is bad, thinks they are 500 mg tablets, and sometimes forgets/skips doses; caregiver said chemist had advised regular dosing four times a day and he skips most of them.
Tramadol was prescribed once in the past but the patient never took it and never filled the prescription.

Naproxen discontinuation reason is not captured with the medication: 500 mg twice daily was stopped because it was burning his stomach; doctor explicitly said not to restart it because of stomach upset.

Examination recorded 'power and feeling in the feet are intact today' but the doctor also said straight leg raise was clear on both sides with no nerve stretch; this absence of nerve stretch signs is partly represented, but the explicit 'today' qualification on intact foot power/sensation is missing.
Doctor stated he was not going to call this anything sinister.
MRI plan was conditional not just on 'not settled in six weeks' generally, but specifically deferred until review if still no better; doctor said not booking it today and 'not before'.
